title: Orbital cut its weekly sync to eleven minutes
description: A ninety-minute all-hands became a page everyone had already read, and the meeting became the argument that was left over.
quote: We stopped writing the same decision down in three places. That is the whole pitch, and it turned out to be worth a headcount.
content:
Orbital's Monday sync was ninety minutes and thirty-one people. Most of it was status: eleven teams saying what they had done, to an audience who mostly needed to know about one of them.

The page came first

The first change had nothing to do with agents. Every team got one page and a rule: the page is written by Friday, the meeting is for what the page could not settle.

This half-worked, in the way it half-works everywhere. Pages got written; nobody read them; the meeting stayed ninety minutes because the first twenty went on catching people up.

Writing it down was never the problem. Reading eleven pages on a Monday morning was the problem.

Then the summary agent

Orbital's operations team wrote a note at the top of the sync page — summarise the eleven team pages, lead with what changed and what slipped — and left it there permanently. An agent picks it up at 06:00 every Monday.

The summary is one page. It cites every claim back to the team page it came from, so anyone who cares about a line can open the source in one click. It goes out at 06:15.

What the meeting is now

Eleven minutes, and it is genuinely a different meeting. The agenda is whatever people left notes on in the summary between six and nine, which is usually two or three real disagreements.

  • Ninety minutes to eleven, measured over six months
  • Thirty-one attendees to nine, with the rest reading the page
  • Around 470 hours a year given back, on Orbital's own arithmetic

The number Rowan Ellery quotes is the headcount one: the operations coordinator role they were about to open was the person who would have been assembling that summary by hand.

title: At Looply, design reviews end in work rather than a document
description: Every review used to produce a doc that nobody opened again. Now it produces notes with owners, and the doc is a by-product.
metricLabel: from review to shipped, down from 3 weeks
quote: The margin notes are the thing. Our reviews used to end in a doc nobody opened again — now they end in work that has an owner.
content:
Looply ran design reviews the way most product companies do: a room, a deck, forty minutes of good discussion, and a note-taker producing a summary that was accurate, thorough and read by nobody.

Counting the leak

They did an audit that is worth stealing. They took six months of review documents, extracted every decision and every action, and checked what had actually happened to each one.

Just over a third of the actions had shipped. Another third had been re-decided later, sometimes the opposite way, by people who did not know the first conversation had happened. The last third had simply evaporated.

Reviewing inside the page

Now the artefact under review is a Margin page, and the review happens in its margin. When somebody says a flow is wrong, they leave a note beside that flow, in the meeting, in about four seconds.

By the end of the review the page carries between eight and twenty notes, each attached to the thing it is about. Assigning them is a pass down the margin that takes two minutes, and nobody retypes anything.

The doc writes itself

The summary document still exists — an agent drafts it from the notes and the page's edit history. It is better than the hand-written one because it links every decision to the block it was about.

But almost nobody reads it, and that is the point. The work is already on a board with owners on it. The document is the record, not the mechanism.

  • Review to shipped: three weeks to four days, median
  • Actions that shipped: 36 per cent to 91 per cent
  • Decisions re-litigated later: down by roughly four fifths

title: Axiom's agents draft every release note before anyone is awake
description: Two engineers used to lose a day a fortnight to release comms. Now they lose ninety seconds each, and the notes are better.
metricLabel: open rate on the release email, from 11%
quote: Our agents draft the changelog, the release notes and half the support replies. We read them. That is a fair trade.
content:
Axiom ships every second Tuesday, and until last year every second Monday was eaten by the same job: turning three weeks of merged pull requests into something a customer would read.

It rotated between two senior engineers. Both of them hated it, both of them were good at it, and the quality visibly fell off in the last third of every set of notes.

What the agent reads

The release agent runs at 06:40 on release Monday. It reads the milestone, the pull requests that actually merged into it, and the last ten published entries — which is where it gets the voice, rather than from a style guide nobody maintains.

It skips reverts, it groups by what a customer can now do rather than by service, and it flags anything it could not describe in one sentence as needing a person. That last behaviour is the one Axiom values most.

It never runs out of care on a Friday. The last three entries are as good as the first three, which was never true when we wrote them.

Ninety seconds each

Two engineers read the draft, usually while the coffee is brewing. The median edit is a sentence, most often to sharpen a claim the agent was too cautious about.

The release email now opens at thirty-four per cent, up from eleven. Replies to it went up roughly six-fold — real questions from real users, which is a category of feedback Axiom did not previously get from release comms at all.

Where it stops

Axiom does not let agents publish. The draft waits for a person, every time, and they have no plans to change that. The saving was never in the clicking.
